mainClaim: Restrictive single-family zoning creates housing shortages, increases inequality, and stifles economic growth
evidence: Hsieh and Moretti (American Economic Journal: Macroeconomics, 2019) argue that high-productivity cities like New York and the San Francisco Bay Area have adopted stringent restrictions on new housing supply, limiting the number of workers who can access that productivity. Using a spatial equilibrium model and data from 220 metropolitan areas, they find that these constraints lowered aggregate US growth by 36 percent from 1964 to 2009.
supportingPoints: Exclusionary zoning perpetuates racial and economic segregation
Artificial scarcity transfers wealth from renters to existing homeowners
Environmental impact: sprawl increases car dependence and emissions

sourceMetadata.title: Housing Constraints and Spatial Misallocation
sourceMetadata.institution: University of Chicago Booth School of Business; University of California, Berkeley
sourceMetadata.methodology: Spatial equilibrium model calibrated on 220 US metropolitan areas

limitations: The 36 percent figure is a model-based counterfactual for US growth from 1964 to 2009, not a measured outcome. Rapid upzoning can cause displacement if not paired with tenant protections. Character preservation has some value. Infrastructure costs need planning. Political implementation extremely difficult due to homeowner opposition.
